title: Class 5: More Data, Better Questions
text:
Google Flu Trends (GFT) offered a compelling shortcut: estimate influenza-like illness from searches before conventional surveillance reports arrived. Ginsberg et al. (2009) reported estimates with roughly a one-day lag. However, searches measure information-seeking, not infections, and the CDC target itself measures the proportion of visits involving influenza-like symptoms, not laboratory-confirmed influenza incidence.
Big data hubris means assuming that abundant digital traces can replace established measurement and analysis. Lazer et al. (2014) reported that GFT overestimated the CDC measure in 100 of 108 weeks beginning in August 2011. More searches did not repair the mismatch between searching and being ill.
Algorithm dynamics make that mismatch unstable. Search suggestions and symptom-related results can change what people search for even without a corresponding change in illness. Lazer and colleagues identify these platform changes as plausible contributors, rather than proving one specific update caused the failure. Deliberate manipulation by users is another possible platform-data problem, although they do not identify it as a GFT explanation.
Transparency and replicability also matter: undisclosed search terms and incomplete methodological detail obstructed independent reconstruction. My takeaway is to preserve model versions, document data processing, and evaluate against external benchmarks. Search data can supplement surveillance, with repeated checks as behavior and platforms change.

title: Class 5: More Data, Better Questions
text:
b. Overfitting and overparameterization
Overfitting occurs when a fitted procedure captures accidental features of its training sample and consequently generalizes poorly. Overparameterization describes a model with more adjustable parameters than the available observations can adequately constrain; in an interpolating regression setting, the parameter count can exceed the sample size. It concerns capacity, whereas overfitting concerns performance. Regularization and other constraints can prevent a highly parameterized model from generalizing badly.
GFT illustrates a related danger in feature selection. The original procedure screened about 50 million candidate queries against a limited CDC series and combined 45 selected queries into one predictor. Its final regression had an intercept and slope, not 50 million fitted coefficients (Ginsberg et al., 2009). Counting only those two coefficients nevertheless misses the flexibility spent selecting the predictor. Lazer et al. describe 1,152 fitting observations and irrelevant seasonal candidates such as high-school basketball. Searching so widely creates opportunities to select coincidences.
This distinction changes how I would validate the analysis: repeat feature selection inside training folds, reserve later time periods for evaluation, and compare with simple seasonal baselines. A successful historical test cannot guarantee robustness to a changed search platform. Overfitting and a shifting data-generating process can coexist.
The R simulation below isolates overfitting using noisy quadratic data. Training error falls with polynomial degree, while error on independently generated test data can rise. These are simulated observations, not GFT estimates; the curve illustrates a mechanism rather than reconstructing Google’s failure.



Training and independent test error for polynomial regressions fitted to simulated quadratic data.

title: Class 5: More Data, Better Questions
text:
c. Wickham talk summary
In his 2019 EMBL keynote, Wickham presents visualization as part of an iterative programming workflow. Technologies include R, RStudio, tidyverse tools, ggplot2, and R Markdown. Techniques include reshaping tidy data, mapping variables to aesthetics, layering plots, adjusting scales, handling overplotting, faceting, animation, and using functions to reduce repetition. His country income and life-expectancy example makes these choices concrete: colour and size add information, while a logarithmic income scale changes what differences are visible.
The larger point is that reusable components and readable code make exploration easier, while executable reports connect explanations to computations. Visualization and modeling can inform each other: a residual plot may reveal a pattern that a single error statistic conceals.
I would qualify the emphasis on programming: reproducible code can faithfully reproduce a flawed measurement. For example, a polished chart of campus flu-related searches could reflect an awareness campaign rather than an outbreak. Wickham’s workflow helps expose analytical choices, but the GFT case shows why those choices still require substantive knowledge and independent validation.

title: Class 3: From Presenting Numbers to Building Understanding
text:
After reading the video summary and website introduction for Journalism in the Age of Data, my main takeaway is that the value of data visualization goes beyond turning data into attractive graphics. It helps readers understand issues that might otherwise be difficult to see. A chart can capture attention, but if readers finish looking at it without understanding its main point, it may not have achieved its purpose. This made me reconsider what I want to learn in this course. Along with learning how to use visualization tools, I should practice identifying the questions that data can answer and communicating those answers clearly.
I was particularly interested in IBM’s effort to democratize visualization through Many Eyes. Making visualization easier to create gives more people opportunities to explore topics they care about and share their findings. However, I do not think that accessible tools necessarily make data easy to interpret. Even when anyone can generate a chart, they still need to understand how variables are defined, where the data come from, and whether the comparisons are appropriate. Democratizing visualization therefore also requires developing the ability to interpret data, so that people understand what their charts actually represent.
The Martini Glass structure discussed in the summary helped me understand the relationship between storytelling and open exploration more clearly. Guiding readers through the background and main findings before allowing them to explore can keep them from feeling overwhelmed at the beginning. If I were creating an interactive unemployment chart, I would first explain the overall trend, the reporting period, and the definition of the measure. I would then let readers compare different groups. This approach provides direction while leaving room for readers to ask their own questions. However, guidance can also influence their judgment, so I think a visualization should clearly distinguish between what the data show and how the author interprets them.
Another point that stood out to me is that visual appeal and readability do not always go together. A streamgraph of movie box office revenues might convey the overall shape of the data, but readers who want to compare a particular movie’s revenue over time may need a chart that makes individual values easier to read. This reminds me that a chart is not necessarily appropriate just because it looks innovative. Before designing a visualization, I should identify what readers need to do: compare values, observe trends, or understand a distribution. A chart’s success should depend on how well it supports those tasks.
The journalism examples also helped me recognize that visualization is the result of a series of editorial decisions. Organizing data, choosing comparisons, and writing titles and annotations all influence what readers see. Removing some information can reduce the burden on readers, but leaving out important context can also be misleading. For example, when presenting death counts across different regions, I should consider how population size affects the comparison, rather than looking only at totals. I believe an effective visualization needs a clear focus while also explaining relevant limitations, so that readers can assess the conclusions it supports.
The discussion of data openness and completeness reminded me that having access to data does not mean having the whole picture. If certain categories are missing, a blank area in a chart may reflect a lack of records rather than the absence of events. Before creating a visualization, I should check which periods, locations, and populations the data cover, and distinguish between zero values and missing values. This is especially important for topics such as crime, unemployment, and war casualties, where the numbers represent real people and their lives.
The website states that the video was produced in 2009–2010, so I understand its discussion of Flash and other tools within that historical context. More useful to me than remembering a particular software name is learning how creators handle data that continue to change. For example, if an unusually high value appears in a chart that updates in real time, will the original axis range still work? Although automatic updates can save time, creators still need to anticipate exceptional cases and establish appropriate checks.
The most practical lesson I take from this material is to begin future class assignments by writing down a question I want to answer, and then deciding which data and charts to use. I also want to practice expressing the main finding in a single sentence and asking someone unfamiliar with the data to review the visualization. If that person has to work hard to guess what the chart means, I will know that it needs revision. My goal is to create work that helps readers understand an issue and recognize the evidence and limitations behind that understanding.

Reference: Geoff McGhee, Journalism in the Age of Data. The video introduction page lists the production period as 2009–2010 and the running time as 54 minutes.

title: Class 2: Huang’s Data Guide
text:
A personal checklist for inspecting a dataset before I analyze or visualize it. Adapted from the Quartz Bad Data Guide (Christopher Groskopf and contributors, CC BY-NC 4.0) and organized by who can fix the problem, with extra items for the two kinds of data I work with: gridded weather reanalysis and medical imaging datasets.
Prepared for EPPS 6356 Data Visualization (Prepare for Class 2), Fall 2026.

title: Class 2: Huang’s Data Guide
text:
How I use this
I do not walk through all 60 items every time. I run Tier 1 on every new dataset (15 minutes), then go to the section that matches whatever looks wrong.
Tier 1 — always, before anything else

How many rows and columns do I have, and how many did I expect?
What does one row represent? (one station-hour? one patient? one image?)
Print summary() / describe() for every column: min, max, mean, NA count.
Plot every variable at least once — histogram for continuous, bar for categorical, time series for anything dated. (Anscombe 1973: summary statistics alone will not show me the structure.)
Where did this file come from, who made it, and when was it last updated?

title: Class 2: Huang’s Data Guide
text:
1. Problems my source should solve
If these appear, I go back and ask, rather than patching the data myself.

Missing values — are blanks / null “no measurement taken”, “refused to answer”, or “zero”? These are not the same thing.
Missing values replaced by zeros — a run of 0 or -1 in a numeric column, 1970-01-01 or 1969-12-31 in a date column, 0°N 0°E in coordinates (Null Island). Very common in sensor data.
Rows or values duplicated — is a repeated ID a real correction, or a merge that ran twice?
Data are obviously incomplete — 48 of 50 states, 11 of 12 months, a patient cohort missing a whole site.
Inconsistent spelling / name order / date formats — a sign the data were typed by a human.
Units are not labeled — °C or K? mm or inches? mm or pixels?
Categories are badly chosen or field names are ambiguous.
The provenance is not documented.
Values are impossible (negative rainfall, age 200, patient height 3 m).
Data are too coarse — monthly means when I need daily; county totals when I need tracts.
The published total does not match the file — recount and compare.
The file has exactly 65,536 rows / 255 columns — it was truncated by an old Excel limit.
Text became numbers, or numbers became text — leading zeros gone, IDs in scientific notation.

title: Class 2: Huang’s Data Guide
text:
2. Problems I should solve myself

Garbled characters (mojibake) — encoding is not UTF-8; fix the encoding rather than the characters.
Line endings are broken — CRLF vs LF. I hit exactly this in my Quarto repository, where every file showed as modified.
The data are locked inside a PDF — extract with a tool, never retype.
The data are too granular — aggregate rather than plotting 10 million points.
The data were entered by hand — spot-check a sample against the source.
Formats and annotations are mixed into the cells — footnote markers, thousands separators, “N/A” as text.
My calculation ignored missing values — did the mean silently drop them, or treat them as zero?
The sample is not random, or is biased toward one group.
The margin of error is too large, or is unknown — if I cannot state it, I say so in the chart.
The data were edited by hand — keep the original file untouched and script every change, so the cleaning is reproducible.
Inflation, seasonality, or population growth distorts the comparison — adjust before comparing across years.
The time frame or the reference category was changed mid-series — a break in a time series is not a trend.

title: Class 2: Huang’s Data Guide
section: 3. Problems an expert should help me solve
text:
3. Problems an expert should help me solve

The author is not trustworthy — who benefits from this result?
The collection process is opaque — no methodology section, no codebook.
The data are suspiciously precise — 6 decimal places from an instrument accurate to 0.5.
There are unexplained outliers — real event, or sensor failure?
The index is meaningless — composite indices hide their weights. (The Happy Planet Index in Assignment 2 is exactly this kind of number.)
The significance test looks wrong — p-hacking, no correction for multiple comparisons.
The data violate Benford’s Law, or are too good to be true — possible fabrication.

title: Class 2: Huang’s Data Guide
section: 4. Problems a programmer should help me solve
text:
4. Problems a programmer should help me solve

Data were merged on the wrong key — row counts change after a join; always check before and after.
The data are inside scanned images — OCR is needed, and OCR makes mistakes.

title: Class 2: Huang’s Data Guide
text:
5. My own additions

Weather and climate data (ERA5, station records)

Time zone and reference time — is the timestamp UTC or local? Is “daily” midnight-to-midnight in which zone?
Gaps in the series — a missing hour is invisible in a line chart because the line simply connects across it. Count gaps explicitly.
Units and sign conventions — K vs °C, Pa vs hPa, accumulated vs instantaneous fields, wind direction “from” vs “toward”.
Grid and resolution — what is the cell size, and does the grid match between variables before I stack them?
Longitude convention — 0–360 or −180–180? A wrong convention silently moves the map.
Reanalysis is a model output, not an observation — it is interpolated, and should be described that way in captions.
Version changes — a re-release of the same product can change values for past dates.



Medical imaging datasets (X-ray)

Label definitions — what exactly counts as positive, and who decided?
Label source — expert reading, or text mined from reports?
Multiple images per patient — splitting by image instead of by patient leaks data between train and test sets.
Site and device differences — resolution, contrast, and orientation vary by hospital and scanner.
Class imbalance — a rare finding makes accuracy meaningless.
Preprocessing already applied — has the image been cropped, windowed, or normalized before I received it?
Ordinal labels treated as categories — severity grades have an order, and the visualization should keep it.



Before I publish a chart

Does the chart state its source and the date of the data?
Are units on the axis?
Does the axis start at zero, and if not, is that justified and visible?
Is uncertainty shown, or at least mentioned?
Would the chart still be honest if someone read only the title?

title: EPPS 6356 Assignment 3: Anatomy of a Chart
text:
1. Documenting a chart
I chose the scatterplot panel from examples-stdplots.R in chapter 1 of Murrell’s R Graphics, because it is the only one of the six that never calls a high-level function. It builds the whole figure from plot.new() and plot.window() plus low-level calls, which makes every ingredient of a plot visible. The comment on each call says what that call contributes to the finished figure.

x  <- c(0.5, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16)       # travel time in seconds: the x positions
y1 <- c(1, 1.3, 1.9, 3.4, 3.9, 4.8) # responses per travel: the rising series
y2 <- c(4, .8, .5, .45, .4, .3)     # responses per second: the falling series

op <- par(las = 1,                  # tick labels horizontal, so the right axis reads easily
          mar = c(4, 4, 2, 4),      # extra space on the RIGHT for the second y axis
          cex = .7)                 # shrink all text so the panel is not crowded

plot.new()                          # opens an empty plot region; draws nothing at all
plot.window(range(x), c(0, 6))      # fixes the coordinate system: x from the data, y from 0 to 6

lines(x, y1)                        # the line carries the trend between the six
lines(x, y2)                        # discrete observations, which points alone cannot show
points(x, y1, pch = 16, cex = 2)    # solid circles: the rising series
points(x, y2, pch = 21, bg = "white", cex = 2)
                                    # open circles drawn over the line, so each marker hides
                                    # the line behind it and the two series stay separable

par(col = "gray50", fg = "gray50", col.axis = "gray50")
                                    # everything from here on is grey, so the frame recedes
                                    # and the black data stays dominant

axis(1, at = seq(0, 16, 4))         # bottom axis; ticks chosen by hand, not by R's default
axis(2, at = seq(0, 6, 2))          # left axis, read against "responses per travel"
axis(4, at = seq(0, 6, 2))          # the two series share a numeric range but measure
                                    # different quantities, so each gets its own labelled axis
box(bty = "u")                      # frame on three sides only; the top stays open

mtext("Travel Time (s)", side = 1, line = 2, cex = 0.8)
mtext("Responses per Travel", side = 2, line = 2, las = 0, cex = 0.8)
                                    # las = 0 turns this label vertical, parallel to its axis
mtext("Responses per Second", side = 4, line = 2, las = 0, cex = 0.8)
text(4, 5, "Bird 131")              # text() places a string INSIDE the plot region at data
                                    # coordinates; mtext() places strings in the margins
par(op)                             # restores the settings so the next figure starts clean







Figure 1: The scatterplot panel from Murrell’s chapter 1, with a comment per call.

Comparing ways of drawing them

       pch = pchs[i], col = cols[i], cex = 1.4,
       xlab = paste0("x", i), ylab = paste0("y", i),

  abline(fits[[i]], col = cols[i], lty = ltys[i], lwd = 2)

Figure 2: The same four fits, drawn with a different colour, line type and plotting character each.





The two tables above show that all four data sets share the same intercept (3.00), slope (0.50), R² (0.6665) and almost identical residual standard errors, alongside means, variances and correlations that agree to two decimal places. Judged by these numbers alone, they appear to be the same data set repeated four times. The scatterplots show otherwise. Data set 1 is the roughly linear relationship the statistics imply, while data set 2 follows a smooth curve that a straight line cannot represent. Data set 3 is an almost perfect linear relationship whose fitted line is dragged away from it by a single outlier, and in data set 4 the slope is an artifact: every x is 8 except one observation at 19, so that one point alone determines the line. Summary statistics can quantify the magnitude of a relationship, but they are blind to its shape and highly vulnerable to the leverage of isolated points. The remedy is to make graphing part of the modelling process rather than a postscript: plot the raw data before fitting anything, examine the residuals against the fitted values afterwards, and transform a variable or add a quadratic term when the pattern turns out to be curved. When a single observation dictates the result, the most transparent approach is to report the model both with and without it, so the reader can see how much the conclusion rests on that one point.

3. Finetuning without leaving base R
Three changes, base graphics only: a serif font, a palette of my own, and my own plotting character. pch accepts a literal character, so the marker is a glyph I chose rather than one of R’s 25 numbered symbols.

ink    <- "#2F3E46"; accent <- "#A63A2E"
panel  <- "#FBF7F0"; grid   <- "#CBD5D1"
fit1 <- lm(y1 ~ x1, data = anscombe)

op <- par(family = "serif", bg = panel, fg = ink,
          col.axis = ink, col.lab = ink, col.main = ink,
          mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1.5), las = 1)

plot(anscombe$x1, anscombe$y1, type = "n",
     xlim = c(3, 20), ylim = c(3, 13),
     xlab = "x1", ylab = "y1",
     main = "Anscombe data set 1, tuned in base R", bty = "n")
abline(h = seq(4, 12, 2), col = grid, lwd = 0.8)
abline(v = seq(4, 20, 4), col = grid, lwd = 0.8)
abline(fit1, col = accent, lwd = 2)
points(anscombe$x1, anscombe$y1, pch = "✦", col = ink, cex = 1.3)
box(bty = "l", col = ink)
mtext("Fitted line: y = 3.00 + 0.50x", side = 3, line = 0.2,
      adj = 0, cex = 0.8, col = accent)
par(op)

No equivalent, or works differently

par(mfrow = c(2, 2)): ggplot2 has no device-level layout. The nearest equivalents are facet_wrap() for the same plot over different subsets, or an external package such as patchwork for different plots side by side.
op <- par(...) and par(op): there is nothing to restore. A ggplot carries its own theme, so settings never leak into the next figure.
Drawing order: in base R the order of the calls is the z-order; in ggplot2 the order of the layers in the + chain does that job, and the whole plot is assembled before anything is drawn.

In base R, abline() draws an unbounded line across the plot region, because it represents the fitted equation rather than the fitted values. In ggplot2, geom_smooth() is a layer computed over the range of the data, so the line stops at the first and last observation unless fullrange = TRUE is set. The two figures therefore encode the same model but make different claims about where that model applies.

text:
5. Replicating the COVID chart
Daily COVID deaths in Europe, one point per country per day, from the Our World in Data frozen snapshot. The file is about 94 MB, so it is not kept in this repository; the code below downloads it once and works from the local copy.

# Daily COVID counts, Our World in Data (frozen snapshot).
url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/owid/covid-19-data/",
              "master/public/data/owid-covid-data.csv")
download.file(url, "owid-covid-data.csv", mode = "wb")
owidall <- read.csv("owid-covid-data.csv")

owidall <- owidall[!grepl("^OWID", owidall$iso_code), ]   # drop aggregate rows
owideu  <- subset(owidall, continent == "Europe")

owideu$date <- as.Date(owideu$date)
d <- owideu[!is.na(owideu$new_deaths), c("location", "date", "new_deaths")]
d <- d[d$new_deaths >= 0, ]                               # a few negative corrections exist
d <- d[d$date <= as.Date("2023-08-31"), ]                 # the window shown in the target

# The labels are not a legend: take the highest points in each six-month window,
# then drop any country already labelled within the previous four months, so one
# bad spike does not claim every label.
chunks <- split(d, cut(d$date, breaks = "6 months"))
cands  <- do.call(rbind, lapply(chunks, function(ch)
  if (nrow(ch)) ch[order(-ch$new_deaths), ][1:3, ] else NULL))
cands  <- cands[!is.na(cands$location), ]
cands  <- cands[order(-cands$new_deaths), ]

lab <- cands[0, ]
for (i in seq_len(nrow(cands))) {
  same <- lab$location == cands$location[i] &
          abs(as.numeric(lab$date - cands$date[i])) < 120
  if (!any(same)) lab <- rbind(lab, cands[i, ])
}
lab <- head(lab[order(-lab$new_deaths), ], 6)

draw_chart <- function() {
  op <- par(mar = c(6.5, 4.5, 1, 1), las = 1)
  plot(d$date, d$new_deaths, pch = 20, cex = 0.45,
       col = "magenta3",                       # the single non-default colour
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  axis(2, at = c(0, 1000, 3000, 5000))
  mtext("COVID Deaths in Europe (Daily)", side = 2, line = 3, las = 0)
  ticks <- seq(as.Date("2020-01-01"), max(d$date), by = "2 months")
  axis(1, at = ticks, labels = format(ticks, "%Y-%m"), las = 2, cex.axis = 0.65)
  mtext("Date", side = 1, line = 5)
  box()
  text(lab$date, lab$new_deaths, labels = lab$location, pos = 4, cex = 0.75, xpd = NA)
  par(op)
}

draw_chart()                                   # preview
png("covid-europe.png", width = 1200, height = 750, res = 120)
draw_chart()                                   # same function, so the export matches the preview
dev.off()




Daily COVID deaths in Europe, 2020–2023. One point per country per day; the six highest points are labelled with the country name.


Three notes on the replication. The labels are placed with text() at the data coordinates of the points themselves, not with legend() — a legend would map colours to countries, which is not what the target does. The date axis is drawn by hand with axis() so the ticks fall every two months and las = 2 turns the labels upright. Wrapping the plotting code in a function means the preview and the exported PNG are produced by the same code, so the file cannot drift from what I checked on screen.

text:
Anscombe’s four regression data sets


Anscombe’s quartet (Anscombe 1973) shows that summary statistics can oversimplify data. The four data sets share nearly identical statistical properties: the mean of x is 9, the mean of y is 7.5, the correlation is 0.816, and every fitted regression line is y = 3 + 0.5x with an R² of 0.67. Because these numbers are only summaries, they suggest the four data sets are the same. The scatter plots, however, reveal four different structures: data set 1 is roughly linear, data set 2 is clearly curved, data set 3 is a near-perfect line distorted by one outlier, and in data set 4 a single extreme point creates the entire slope. A linear regression is only appropriate for the first case. Anscombe’s own solution is to make both calculations and graphs: scatterplot the data before any regression, plot the residuals against the fitted values after fitting, transform the variables or add a quadratic term when the relation is curved (data set 2), check whether outliers are recording errors (data set 3), and when one observation strongly influences the result, report the regression both with and without it (data set 4).

3. Chart Critique



Market Capitalization of the World’s Biggest Banks. Source: Cairo (2012), Figure 2.8.


This chart uses nested bubbles to compare the market value of 15 banks in January 2007 and January 2009. The problem is that people judge length much more accurately than area. For example, Société Générale’s value fell from $80 billion to $26 billion, but it is hard to tell from the bubbles that the inner circle is only about one-third of the outer one. As Cairo shows, a bar chart makes this comparison much easier. Bubble charts are popular and look attractive, but designers often choose them by following trends rather than asking what the reader needs to see.
I would go one step further. The real story in this data is how much each bank lost, yet neither the bubble chart nor a simple bar chart shows the percentage decline directly. RBS lost 96% of its value, Citigroup 93%, and Barclays 92%, while Santander lost only 45%. These differences are almost invisible in the bubbles. A bar chart of percentage change, sorted from largest to smallest loss, or a dumbbell chart connecting the 2007 and 2009 values, would let readers see immediately which banks were hit hardest by the financial crisis.

title: EPPS 6356 Assignment 2: Base R Graphics
text:
1. Working through Murrell’s chapter 1 code
The opening examples helped me understand the difference between starting a plot and adding to one. A high-level call such as plot() normally creates a new plot, establishes coordinates, and draws the data, axes, frame, and labels. The scatterplot panel in the standard-plot examples separates these steps: plot.new() opens a blank plot, plot.window() establishes the coordinate ranges, and low-level calls supply the lines, points, axes, frame, and text. This makes the work that a single plot() call normally handles much easier to see.
par() changes the graphics settings rather than drawing observations. For example, mfrow determines how subsequent plots share the device, mar reserves space around each plot, and las controls the orientation of axis labels. These changes become visible when the relevant elements are drawn. Saving the previous settings and restoring them afterward matters because otherwise a later plot may inherit margins, colors, or a layout intended for an earlier example.
The order of commands is especially important in base graphics. My notes initially described the text as simply not appearing when text() came before plot(), but the more precise explanation depends on the device state: without an existing plot, text() produces an error; with one, it adds text to that plot, which a subsequent high-level call can replace. Base graphics draws onto the current device as commands execute, so changing an earlier element usually means drawing the plot again. In ggplot2, layers and settings are normally assembled into a plot object before that object is printed.
Two examples corrected my initial interpretation of the code. In the histogram, freq = FALSE puts the bars on a probability-density scale so that the dnorm() curve uses the same units; a density curve over a count histogram would usually appear compressed near the baseline. Also, boxplot() normally starts a new plot, but boxplot(add = TRUE) adds boxes to the existing coordinates. The function’s behavior therefore depends on its arguments, and the two offset sets of boxes can appear side by side without erasing each other.
The bar-chart example showed that a plotting function can also return useful information. barplot() returns the bar midpoints, which the later mtext() and text() calls use to align labels with the bars. This also clarified the difference between text positioned in the margins and text placed at data coordinates inside the plot. For the surface example, theta changes the horizontal viewing direction, phi changes the viewing elevation, and expand controls the relative height of the surface.
My recorded work covers the introduction and standard base-graphics examples. The notes do not document completed runs of the later lattice, ggplot2, or other package-dependent sections, so I do not report those sections as completed. Those examples require additional plotting systems, packages, or image resources; the discussion here is limited to what the base-graphics notes support.

title: EPPS 6356 Assignment 2: Base R Graphics
text:
2. The plotting functions
Each function below is used on the 2024 Happy Planet Index data. The code that produced every figure is shown with it. The final five examples build up the same GDP–life satisfaction comparison, redrawing the plot in each chunk so that every figure is reproducible.

2.1 Setting up the canvas

par()

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4, 1, 1), las = 1)
hist(hpi$life_exp, breaks = 12, col = "grey80", main = "",
     xlab = "Life expectancy (years), 2024")
hist(hpi$hpi, breaks = 12, col = "lightblue", main = "",
     xlab = "Happy Planet Index, 2024")
par(op)







Figure 1: par() draws nothing itself: it sets the layout, margins, and axis-label orientation that later calls use, which only becomes visible once the two histograms are drawn into the 1 x 2 layout.







box()

plot(hpi$life_exp, hpi$hpi, bty = "n", pch = 16,
     col = "steelblue", xlab = "Life expectancy (years), 2024",
     ylab = "Happy Planet Index, 2024")
box(bty = "l", col = "grey30", lwd = 2)







Figure 2: box() adds a frame to an existing plot; bty = ‘l’ draws only its left and bottom edges.







axis()

plot(hpi$life_exp, hpi$hpi, axes = FALSE, pch = 16,
     col = "steelblue", xlab = "Life expectancy (years), 2024",
     ylab = "Happy Planet Index, 2024")
axis(1, at = seq(50, 90, 10), labels = paste(seq(50, 90, 10), "yr"))
axis(2, at = seq(0, 80, 20), las = 1)
box(bty = "l")







Figure 3: axis() adds axes to an existing plot and controls their sides, tick positions, labels, and label orientation.








2.2 Drawing whole plots

hist()

hist(hpi$life_exp, breaks = 12, col = "grey80", main = "",
     xlab = "Life expectancy (years), 2024")







Figure 4: hist() starts a new plot and groups life expectancy into bins whose bar heights show the number of countries in each interval.







boxplot()

op <- par(mar = c(4.5, 13, 1, 1))
boxplot(hpi ~ continent, data = hpi, horizontal = TRUE,
        las = 1, col = "lightblue", main = "", ylab = "",
        xlab = "Happy Planet Index, 2024", cex.axis = 0.8)
par(op)







Figure 5: boxplot() compares regional HPI distributions through medians, quartiles, whiskers extending to observations within 1.5 interquartile ranges, and points beyond the whiskers.







pie()

region_counts <- table(hpi$continent)
region_labels <- paste0(names(region_counts), " (", region_counts, ")")
pie(region_counts, labels = region_labels,
    col = hcl.colors(length(region_counts), "Pastel 1"),
    radius = 0.65, cex = 0.7, main = "Countries by region, 2024")







Figure 6: pie() shows each region’s share of the 153 country records as a slice, although a bar chart would make comparisons easier because lengths are easier to compare than angles or areas.







persp()

surface_data <- hpi[complete.cases(hpi[c("hpi", "life_exp", "footprint")]), ]
surface_model <- lm(hpi ~ life_exp + footprint, data = surface_data)
xs <- seq(min(surface_data$life_exp), max(surface_data$life_exp), length.out = 30)
ys <- seq(min(surface_data$footprint), max(surface_data$footprint), length.out = 30)
grid <- expand.grid(life_exp = xs, footprint = ys)
z <- matrix(predict(surface_model, newdata = grid), nrow = length(xs))
persp(xs, ys, z, theta = 35, phi = 25, expand = 0.5,
      col = "lightblue", shade = 0.3, ticktype = "detailed",
      xlab = "Life expectancy", ylab = "Footprint", zlab = "Fitted HPI",
      cex.axis = 0.65, cex.lab = 0.8)







Figure 7: persp() projects a grid of fitted HPI values into a three-dimensional surface with a chosen viewing angle; this illustrative linear-model surface is not raw country data or the HPI formula, and some grid combinations may lack observations.





Life expectancy is measured in years and ecological footprint in global hectares per person. The fitted surface is a descriptive graphics demonstration, not a causal model.



2.3 Adding to an existing plot

points()

scatter <- hpi[complete.cases(hpi[c("gdp", "life_sat")]) &
                 hpi$continent %in% c("East Asia", "Western Europe"), ]
scatter$gdp_thousands <- scatter$gdp / 1000
regions <- c("East Asia", "Western Europe")
region_colors <- c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")
region_symbols <- c(16, 17)
group_id <- match(scatter$continent, regions)

# Reuse the same background and points in the following examples.
draw_scatter <- function() {
  plot(scatter$gdp_thousands, scatter$life_sat, type = "n",
       xlab = "GDP per capita (thousands, PPP international dollars), 2024",
       ylab = "Life satisfaction (0-10), 2024", ylim = c(3, 9))
  points(scatter$gdp_thousands, scatter$life_sat,
         col = region_colors[group_id], pch = region_symbols[group_id])
}
draw_scatter()







Figure 8: points() adds country observations to an existing coordinate system, using blue circles for East Asia and orange triangles for Western Europe.







lines()

trend <- lowess(scatter$gdp_thousands, scatter$life_sat)
draw_scatter()
lines(trend, col = "grey30", lwd = 2)







Figure 9: lines() connects ordered coordinates on an existing plot, here adding a LOWESS trend for the two displayed regions pooled together.








2.4 Annotating

text()

label_rows <- unique(c(which.min(scatter$life_sat), which.max(scatter$life_sat)))
add_country_labels <- function() {
  text(scatter$gdp_thousands[label_rows], scatter$life_sat[label_rows],
       labels = scatter$country[label_rows], pos = c(1, 3), cex = 0.8)
}
draw_scatter()
lines(trend, col = "grey30", lwd = 2)
add_country_labels()







Figure 10: text() places country labels at data coordinates inside the existing plot, here identifying the highest and lowest life satisfaction among the displayed countries.







mtext()

op <- par(mar = c(6, 4.5, 2, 1))
draw_scatter()
lines(trend, col = "grey30", lwd = 2)
add_country_labels()
mtext("Source: Happy Planet Index 2026; observations from 2024",
      side = 1, line = 4.5, cex = 0.8)
par(op)







Figure 11: mtext() adds a source note in the plot margin using a side and line offset, whereas text() positions labels using data coordinates.







legend()

op <- par(mar = c(6, 4.5, 2, 1))
draw_scatter()
lines(trend, col = "grey30", lwd = 2)
add_country_labels()
mtext("Source: Happy Planet Index 2026; observations from 2024",
      side = 1, line = 4.5, cex = 0.8)
legend("topright", legend = c(regions, "Pooled LOWESS trend"),
       col = c(region_colors, "grey30"), pch = c(region_symbols, NA),
       lty = c(NA, NA, 1), lwd = c(NA, NA, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(op)







Figure 12: legend() explains the colors, point symbols, and fitted line used in the existing plot.








A note on names()
names() is not a plotting function: it reads or sets an object’s names attribute, which functions such as pie() and barplot() can use as labels. It belongs to data preparation rather than drawing on a graphics device.

text:
Chart 4: one variable across a few items
Abela’s Chart Thought-Starter sends a comparison of one variable among a few items to a column chart, so that is what the brief called for. The variable is the Happy Planet Index; the items are the five continents.



Mean Happy Planet Index by continent, 2024. Columns ordered from highest to lowest mean; the white label inside each column gives the number of countries behind the mean.



The code

df_chart4 <- hpi_clean |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(mean_hpi = mean(hpi, na.rm = TRUE),
            n        = dplyr::n(),
            .groups  = "drop") |>
  mutate(continent_ordered = fct_reorder(continent, mean_hpi, .desc = TRUE))

p4 <- ggplot(df_chart4,
             aes(x = continent_ordered, y = mean_hpi, fill = continent)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.68, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", mean_hpi)),
            vjust = -0.55, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_text(aes(y = 1.8, label = paste0("n = ", n)),
            size = 2.9, colour = "#FFFFFF", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_continent() +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Mean Happy Planet Index Score (0-100 Scale)",
                     limits = c(0, 62), breaks = seq(0, 60, by = 10),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  theme_hackathon(legend_pos = "none")

The full script is assignments/Chart4.R in the team repository.


Three decisions behind the chart
The bars start at zero and the axis says so. A column encodes a quantity by length, so a truncated baseline makes the lengths lie. limits = c(0, 62) with expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02)) pins the columns to the axis line instead of floating them above it.
The columns are sorted, not alphabetical. Alphabetical order would be a second, irrelevant variable competing with the one the reader came for. Sorting by the mean turns the ranking into something read at a glance, which is the cheapest comparison in Cleveland and McGill’s hierarchy — position along a common scale.
The chart states its own n. A continental mean hides how many countries it averages: Oceania’s mean rests on a handful of countries, Africa’s on dozens. The white n = label inside each column puts that caveat where the number is, rather than in a footnote nobody reads.

The image that stayed with me was the Beethoven poster, where the letter E is drawn together with the lines of a musical staff. I did not see the staff at first; it appeared only after I had been looking for a while. That is the point of the film in one image: visual design is not decoration handed to the viewer all at once. Some things have to be looked at for a while before the details come out. Druckrey trains exactly this kind of looking.

title: Class 2: Review of Teaching to See
text:
1. Thin/thick and curve/linearity
The exercises focus on the thick and thin parts of a letter. At first I did not understand why a stroke would be thicker at the ends and thinner in the middle, but the result looks balanced and calm rather than stiff. The variation comes from the writing tool: a broad pen held at a fixed angle produces a wide mark in one direction and a narrow one in the other, so the thickness of a curve changes continuously as it turns. Where a straight stem meets a curve, that transition has to be smoothed by hand, or the letter looks broken. Redrawing the same letter many times is how the students learn to feel where the weight should go.
The work is also about space, not only about the strokes themselves. The Roman alphabet is remarkably symmetrical, and when the students modify an existing typeface, every letter has to be adjusted so that the spaces inside and between the letters stay even. Design has to leave room.

title: Class 2: Review of Teaching to See
text:
2. The eye and the hand
Holmes separates writing into two opposing aspects. The eye is the conservative one: “the eye wants to look at an orderly set of marks on a page — the eye wants pattern,” something regular and reliable. The hand is “the radical aspect of writing”: it wants to move, and to “write faster and faster.” Writing is the negotiation between them.
A signature is where that tension becomes visible. It is produced too quickly for the eye to impose order on it, so what remains is the trace of the hand — which is exactly why a signature is unique and hard to forget. The letterform exercises in the film work in the opposite direction: they slow the hand down until the eye can lead.

title: Class 2: Review of Teaching to See
section: 3. Calligraphy, Steve Jobs, and the Macintosh
text:
3. Calligraphy, Steve Jobs, and the Macintosh
Jobs took a calligraphy class, and the film connects that class to the typography of the Macintosh. What he learned was not only that letters can be beautiful. Calligraphy teaches judgment about proportion, spacing, and the small visual corrections that make a line of text read well. When the Macintosh shipped with proportionally spaced fonts and careful letterforms, it carried that judgment into a machine, and from there into everything that was made with it.

title: Class 2: Review of Teaching to See
text:
4. Geometric accuracy versus optical accuracy
Geometric accuracy and optical accuracy are not the same thing. A letter can be measured and constructed so that every dimension is exactly equal, and it will still look wrong to the eye — a little heavy here, a little short there. The eye does not measure; it compares, and it is easily misled by shape. So the designer deliberately introduces small deviations from the geometry until the letter looks right, and at that point the viewer accepts it as correct without noticing that anything was changed.
The thinning of a stem toward its middle, which I described above, is one of these corrections: geometrically the stroke is no longer of even width, but optically it reads as straighter and steadier than a stroke of constant width.
The same judgment governs the alphabet as a whole. In the film the students work toward three things at once. First, the letters have to share a common structure, so that they read as one alphabet rather than a collection of separate drawings. Second, each letter has to stay different enough from every other letter to remain legible — the shared structure cannot be pushed so far that an a starts to look like an o. Third, the spacing between letters has to produce an even rhythm and an even color on the page.
Spacing is the clearest case of optical over geometric accuracy. Equal measured gaps do not look equal, because the shapes on either side differ: the space between two straight stems and the space beside a round or diagonal letter are measured the same and seen differently. The spacing is therefore set by eye until the line of text has an even texture, not by making the distances equal.
This is why Druckrey’s students correct their letters by eye rather than by ruler. Being measurably right is not the goal; being read correctly is.

title: Class 2: Review of Teaching to See
section: What this means for data visualization
text:
What this means for data visualization
Druckrey’s students spend hours on one letter, redrawing it and adjusting the space around it. That is the same work we do when we choose an axis range, a color, or how much white space a chart gets. In both cases the measurement is not the goal — being read correctly is. A chart can be geometrically accurate, with every value plotted exactly, and still be read wrongly, in the same way that a geometrically perfect letter can look wrong. Anscombe’s quartet is the statistical version of the same lesson, and the bubble chart I critiqued in Assignment 1 is the visual one: the circles were scaled correctly by area, yet readers still could not see how much the banks had lost.
Learning to see is learning to check what the reader’s eye actually receives, not what the number says should be there.

title: Class 4: Reflection on Data Analysis and Visualization
text:
The idea that stood out to me most in this video is that the purpose of data analysis is to “get it right.” Analysts must continually ask whether their evidence actually supports their conclusions. In the context of our data visualization course, this means that a chart should be evaluated by how well it helps readers understand a phenomenon, make meaningful comparisons, and recognize the limits of an interpretation. Attractive colors and polished graphics cannot compensate for unreliable data or selective analysis. They may even make a misleading conclusion more persuasive.
The discussion of Google Flu illustrates the danger of overfitting. A model that fits existing observations well may still perform poorly when applied to new situations. This makes the distinction between exploratory and confirmatory research especially useful. Exploring different variables and patterns can generate valuable questions, but those discoveries require further testing with independent evidence. Specifying an analysis in advance helps prevent researchers from changing their questions after seeing the results. For me, the lesson is to be clear about whether an analysis is generating a hypothesis or testing one.
Another important takeaway is that reliable analysis begins with understanding how data were collected. Missing values, spreadsheet conversions, sampling decisions, and the incentives of data providers can all shape the patterns that eventually appear in a visualization. In future assignments, I should examine variable definitions and document which observations were excluded before drawing conclusions. The same critical attitude should apply to the video’s striking examples of research failures: I should ask about their original evidence and scope rather than accept them simply because the presentation is convincing.
For visualization design, the question “Compared to what?” provides a practical starting point. A single number or rising line often means little without a relevant baseline, another group, or a longer time period. The discussion of information-rich displays also challenges the assumption that simpler graphics are always better. Removing clutter can improve understanding, but removing necessary context can distort it. Clear labels, visual hierarchy, and thoughtful arrangement can help readers examine both broad patterns and specific details. A visualization should also avoid implying that an observed association establishes causation.
Ultimately, I want to make “How do I know that?” a regular part of my analytical process. Before creating a chart, I should define the question, identify an appropriate comparison, and record the reasoning behind data-cleaning and analytical choices. Afterward, I should check whether the conclusion goes beyond what the evidence supports. When the available data cannot answer the question, acknowledging that uncertainty is part of doing the work well. Responsible visualization helps readers understand both what we have learned and what still needs to be investigated.
